items.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995
items.q: I just recently recorded a CD on Milestone with Turk Mauro

ctx.x: And sometimes when it’s moved into the concert hall, you know, jazz certainly can belong in a concert hall, but it does change it, and maybe not always for the better. I don’t know. When you play for dancing, you can tell right away if you’re doing it right, especially with let’s say the over-50 set, I’ve found that they know the right tempos that they want to dance to. And they know the feel. If you’re doing it right you’ll see it.

You know I met a lot of fans over in Paris recently, playing for dancing. There’s a couple of little dance clubs that I frequent when I’m over there. And you know you hit it right on the head. They know the tempos that they can do their steps to. So why should musicians say well hey, I want to play this song just a little bit brighter to put an edge on the groove for excitement. Why not slow the tempo down where people can really get in the groove of the music and once you flood the dance floor, you have their…

know, and I look at it that I want to see what you’re made of rhythmically. I want to see how you react to the groove a little bit. So I can play the tempo real slow and juicy and get a groove going, and I know that you will not be able to sit still. You have to get up and start moving, even if there’s no dance floor. You know so that mindset is very important when you’re trying to communicate what is considered contemporary music to the younger people today, because they don’t know about Gene Ammons and Sonny…
